title: Verifier‑Augmented vs. LLM‑Only NetOps Agents: A Paired Evaluation on an Action‑Aware Staging Benchmark
abstract: We report a fully preregistered paired evaluation that compared a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline to an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark (ActionAwareStagingBench‑v1). The preregistered design (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) used gpt-5-mini as the generator, deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as runtime validator and post‑hoc scorer, N = 400 paired tasks (800 episodes) and shared_initial_generation semantics (one shared LLM candidate per task). Confirmatory, artifact‑backed outcomes: complete_pairs = 400; baseline_success_count = 400/400; guarded_success_count = 400/400; paired contingency n_11 = 400, n_10 = n_01 = n_00 = 0; paired difference = 0.0; preregistered permutation p = 1.0; exact McNemar p = 1.0; paired bootstrap 95% CI = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729, 10,000 resamples); Cohen's h = 0.0. We emphasize up front that two preregistered design choices — shared_initial_generation (one shared generator output per pair) and reuse of deterministic_netops_validator_v5 as both runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer — produced a ceiling effect that rendered the primary estimand uninformative for this run. We preserve the full execution and analysis artifacts and describe concrete, artifact‑grounded recommendations for benchmark hardening to expose runtime verifier utility.

sections.introduction: Generative large language models (LLMs) are increasingly proposed to translate operator intent into device configurations and to orchestrate staged rollouts (canaries, progressive delivery, rollback). Prior work documents promise in prototype and IaC settings but also highlights gaps in action‑aware evaluation that exercises end‑to‑end rollout semantics, blocking, repair, rollback, and provenance. Motivated by these gaps, we preregistered and executed a paired experiment (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) to test whether adding a deterministic runtime validator to an LLM pipeline increases end‑to‑end safety (safe‑deploy rate) relative to an LLM‑only pipeline. The study used a paired design with N = 400 deterministic intent→configuration tasks, two per‑task conditions (baseline: LLM‑only; guarded: verifier‑augmented), and a shared_initial_generation setting that delivered one identical LLM candidate to both conditions. The central research question was: Under a compact action‑aware staging benchmark, does a verifier‑augmented pipeline increase the paired safe‑deploy rate relative to an LLM‑only pipeline? Our principal contribution is an artifact‑backed, preregistered paired evaluation together with a diagnostic failure analysis that explains why the selected design produced a null/ceiling outcome and provides concrete recommendations for benchmark hardening.
sections.related_work: Intent→configuration translation and intent‑based NetOps have matured through testbeds and prototype systems; recent work demonstrates LLMs can synthesize configuration fragments and templates (intent‑driven configuration, PreConfig, GraphSynth) and that generate–validate–repair patterns help IaC correctness (TerraFormer and related IaC verifier‑guided approaches). Deterministic network verifiers and reachability tools are effective at finding configuration and policy violations in offline and testbed settings. Agentic and tool‑augmented LLM architectures (ReAct, RAG, multi‑agent orchestrations) have been applied to AIOps and NetOps but introduce new failure modes (hallucination, misapplied tools) that motivate runtime guardrails. Surveys and reviews repeatedly call for action‑aware benchmarks that evaluate rollout, blocking, repair, rollback, provenance, and human‑in‑the‑loop tradeoffs; our work operationalizes a compact staging benchmark under a strict preregistered design to probe these questions and to produce reproducible artifacts for follow‑on hardening.
sections.methodology: Preregistration and primary estimand: The preregistration (cnsmauto-3d2k-prereg-v1) specified a paired binary design with exactly N = 400 deterministic tasks generated by deterministic_netops_task_generator_v5. The primary estimand was the paired_success_rate_difference_guarded_minus_baseline; the preregistered primary test was a permutation‑based paired test (two‑sided, α = 0.05). Execution adapter and models: the adapter family was hosted_netops_gvr_v1 and the declared generator was gpt-5-mini (execution/model_configuration.json). The runtime validator and post‑hoc scorer were deterministic_netops_validator_v5. Shared_initial_generation semantics and model‑call accounting: preregistered shared_initial_generation produced one LLM generation per task that was delivered to both conditions; consequently model_calls_used = 400 (one shared generation per task) even though planned_episode_count = 800 (two condition episodes per pair). This choice intentionally isolates validator accept/block/repair behavior on identical generator outputs rather than comparing independent generator variability across conditions. Deterministic consistency and exclusions: deterministic three‑replay consistency checks were preregistered and used; exclusions were defined for nondeterministic runs, simulator errors, or duplicate provenance, with automated handling (no manual adjudication). Repair policy and call budget: the adapter permitted up to one repair call per task (maximum_repair_calls_per_task = 1); repairs could be invoked by the guarded adapter but none were applied in this execution (repair_applied = false). Analysis plan: the preregistered pipeline used paired_binary_analysis_v1 for confirmatory inference; the analysis recorded exact seeds and bootstrap parameters (bootstrap_seed = 1729; resamples = 10,000) and archived all analysis artifacts.
sections.results: Execution and deterministic reconciliation: the run began 2026‑08‑29T18:23:37Z and completed 2026‑08‑29T19:12:38Z. Planned episodes = 800; completed episodes = 800; failed episodes = 0; complete_pairs = 400; model_calls_used = 400 (shared initial generation). Confirmatory outcomes (artifact‑backed): baseline_success_count = 400/400 (success_rate = 1.0); guarded_success_count = 400/400 (success_rate = 1.0). Paired contingency (analysis/paired_contingency_table.csv): n_11 = 400; n_10 = 0; n_01 = 0; n_00 = 0; observed paired difference = 0.0. Statistical inference: the preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0; corroborating exact McNemar two‑sided test returned p = 1.0. Paired bootstrap 95% CI for the paired difference = [0.0, 0.0] (bootstrap_seed = 1729; 10,000 resamples). Effect size: Cohen's h = 0.0. Repair and rollback diagnostics: no runtime repairs or rollbacks occurred across episodes (repair_applied = false); validator traces show deterministic validation_after.final_state = expected_final_state for representative tasks. Representative shared candidate (pair‑000001) was the four‑line configuration sequence shown among archived responses; that shared candidate was accepted by deterministic_netops_validator_v5 in both conditions. Missingness and exclusions: none—complete_pair_count = 400 and deterministic consistency checks passed for all pairs (analysis/deterministic_reconciliation.json).
sections.discussion: Primary interpretation: the observed null/ceiling outcome is a predictable consequence of two preregistered design choices, not evidence that runtime verification is broadly unnecessary. First, shared_initial_generation delivered identical generator outputs to baseline and guarded conditions, removing generation variance as a mechanism for the guarded adapter to change outcomes; second, the runtime guard and post‑hoc scorer were the same deterministic implementation (deterministic_netops_validator_v5), so acceptance decisions and post‑hoc scoring were necessarily concordant. Construct validity consequence: because the same validator accepted the identical shared candidates and also scored outcomes, the experiment measured validator acceptance on identical candidates rather than independent closed‑loop generator+guard dynamics. Statistical and power implications: the preregistered power rationale assumed non‑ceiling baseline rates; the observed ceiling invalidates that rationale for this run and explains the permutation/McNemar results. Practical recommendations for benchmark hardening (artifact‑grounded): (1) remove shared_initial_generation so each condition receives an independent generator output and the guard can veto or request repairs on generator errors; (2) inject targeted adversarial/perturbation task seeds that produce invalid candidates for a controlled fraction of pairs; (3) evaluate heterogeneous generator/validator pairings so runtime guards and scorers are not identical implementations; (4) enable and instrument repair/rollback invocation paths in the adapter to measure how repairs change outcomes. Each recommendation maps directly to artifacts in the archived bundle (task manifests, shared responses, validator traces) and can be operationalized without inventing new datasets.
sections.conclusion: We executed a fully preregistered paired evaluation comparing a verifier‑augmented NetOps pipeline and an LLM‑only pipeline on a compact action‑aware staging benchmark. Under the preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator pairing, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5; both conditions produced 100% safe‑deploy on N = 400 pairs and the preregistered permutation test returned p = 1.0. This ceiling outcome stems from preregistered design choices (shared candidate semantics and reuse of the deterministic validator as both guard and scorer) that removed opportunities for the guard to alter deployments; it therefore does not generalize to heterogeneous generator+guard closed‑loop dynamics. We release the preregistration and full execution/analysis artifacts so researchers can reproduce this run and use the archived artifacts as seeds for hardened experiments (independent per‑condition generation, adversarial injections, or heterogeneous validators) that can expose verifier utility.

limitations: Benchmark hardness and ceiling effect: under preregistered shared_initial_generation semantics and the chosen generator+validator, every shared candidate satisfied deterministic_netops_validator_v5 so the guard had no opportunity to alter outcomes; this makes the primary estimand effectively untestable in this run and invalidates the original power rationale.

Model and scope: experiment used a single generator (gpt-5-mini) and a single deterministic validator (deterministic_netops_validator_v5); results do not generalize across models, validators, or production heterogeneity.

Construct validity: the same deterministic_netops_validator_v5 implementation served as both runtime guard and the post‑hoc scorer; this conflation produces concordant acceptance/scoring and limits inference about independent closed‑loop verifier utility.

Shared candidate semantics: preregistered shared_initial_generation (one LLM generation per task shared by both conditions) intentionally reduces generation variance and therefore limits inference to the validator’s behavior on identical candidates rather than full generator+guard closed‑loop interactions.

Synthetic environment and external validity: the simulator and validator do not fully model production telemetry noise, operator workflows, or adversarial actor behaviours; external validity to live networks is limited.
Adversarial robustness untested: adversarial or distribution‑shifted prompts and generator faults that could trigger guard interventions were not exercised in this run and remain open.

Aggregated difficulty reporting gap: the full per‑task difficulty labels are archived in execution/task_manifest.jsonl; an aggregated histogram by difficulty level for all N = 400 tasks was not summarized in the top‑level manuscript artifacts and therefore remains a preserved reporting limitation (readers can derive the complete aggregation from execution/task_manifest.jsonl in the archived bundle).
